```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", message=FALSE)
has <- function(pkgs) all(vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly=TRUE))
has_mass <- has("MASS")
has_broom <- has_mass && has("broom")
has_emmeans <- has_mass && has("emmeans")
has_sandwich <- has_emmeans && has("sandwich")
has_tidymodels <- has_mass && has(c("parsnip","recipes","workflows","rsample",
                                    "tune","broom"))
```

fastglm supplies methods for generics of three other packages: `tidy()`, `glance()`, and `augment()` of *broom*; `recover_data()` and `emm_basis()` of *emmeans*; and an engine `"fastglm"` for model types of *parsnip*. Each set of methods is registered when the other package is loaded, and none of these packages is required by fastglm. This vignette carries three datasets from *MASS* through them: days absent from school (`quine`, counts), housing satisfaction (`housing`, ordered and unordered categories), and low birth weight (`birthwt`, a binary outcome). Each code chunk runs only when the packages it uses are installed.

# Days absent: Poisson and negative binomial fits

`quine` records the days absent from school of 146 children, with ethnicity (`Eth`), sex (`Sex`), age group (`Age`, four levels), and learner status (`Lrn`). Both models below have the log-linear mean
$$
\log \mu_i = x_i^\top\beta .
$$
The Poisson model sets $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i$; the negative binomial model sets $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i+\mu_i^2/\theta$ and estimates $\theta$ with $\beta$.

```{r quine-fits, eval=has_mass}
library(fastglm)
quine <- MASS::quine
pois <- fastglm(Days ~ Eth + Sex + Age + Lrn, data=quine, family=poisson())
nb <- fastglm_nb(Days ~ Eth + Sex + Age + Lrn, data=quine)
nb$theta
```

`glance()` gives one row per fit. The Poisson residual deviance is more than ten times its residual degrees of freedom, so the Poisson variance is far too small for these data; the negative binomial log likelihood is higher by about 600.

```{r quine-glance, eval=has_broom, warning=FALSE}
library(broom)
rbind(poisson=glance(pois)[c("logLik","AIC","deviance","df.residual")],
      negbin=glance(nb)[c("logLik","AIC","deviance","df.residual")])
```

`tidy()` gives the coefficient table, here with Wald limits and exponentiated to the scale of mean ratios:

```{r quine-tidy, eval=has_broom}
tidy(nb, conf.int=TRUE, exponentiate=TRUE)
```

`augment()` adds fitted values, residuals, and the influence measures of `broom::augment.glm()` (`.hat`, `.sigma`, `.cooksd`, `.std.resid`) to the model frame. With `type.predict="response"`, `.fitted` is $\hat\mu_i$:

```{r quine-augment, eval=has_broom}
aug <- augment(nb, type.predict="response")
head(aug)
```

# Estimated marginal means and contrasts for counts

The reference grid has one cell for each combination of the factor levels, $2\times2\times4\times2=32$ cells here. For the age group $a$, the estimated marginal mean averages the linear predictor over the cells with that age and returns to the mean scale:
$$
\hat m_a=\exp\Big(\frac{1}{|G_a|}\sum_{g\in G_a} x_g^\top\hat\beta\Big),
$$
where $G_a$ is the set of grid cells with age $a$. Contrasts are formed on the log scale, so with `type="response"` a pairwise contrast is a ratio of means $\hat m_a/\hat m_b$. Standard errors use the delta method with the covariance of $\hat\beta$, with $\theta$ treated as known (as for `MASS::glm.nb()` fits).

```{r quine-emmeans, eval=has_emmeans, warning=FALSE}
library(emmeans)
age_nb <- emmeans(nb, "Age", type="response")
age_nb
pairs(age_nb)
```

The Poisson fit is a `glm` object, which *emmeans* handles through its own `glm` support. Its means differ somewhat from those of the negative binomial fit, and its standard errors are a quarter to a third as large, because they use $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i$:

```{r quine-emmeans-poisson, eval=has_emmeans}
age_pois <- emmeans(pois, "Age", type="response")
data.frame(Age=levels(quine$Age),
           mean_poisson=summary(age_pois)$rate, mean_negbin=summary(age_nb)$response,
           se_poisson=summary(age_pois)$SE, se_negbin=summary(age_nb)$SE)
```

Any covariance of the coefficients can replace the model-based one through the `vcov.` argument. The sandwich covariance of the negative binomial fit (HC0, the default of `sandwich::vcovHC()` for fastglm count models) gives standard errors that do not rely on the variance function:

```{r quine-emmeans-sandwich, eval=has_sandwich}
emmeans(nb, "Age", type="response", vcov.=sandwich::vcovHC(nb))
```

Comparisons with a control group use the same interface; here each age group is compared with the youngest (`F0`):

```{r quine-emmeans-control, eval=has_emmeans}
contrast(age_nb, "trt.vs.ctrl")
```

# Ordered satisfaction: cumulative-link probabilities

`housing` gives the satisfaction (`Sat`: low, medium, high) of 1681 residents, recorded as frequencies (`Freq`) in 72 cells defined by perceived influence (`Infl`), housing type (`Type`), and contact with other residents (`Cont`). The proportional odds model is
$$
P(Y_i\le j\mid x_i)=F(\alpha_j-x_i^\top\beta),\qquad j=1,2,
$$
with $F$ the logistic distribution function and cutpoints $\alpha_1<\alpha_2$, so that
$$
P(Y_i=j\mid x_i)=F(\alpha_j-x_i^\top\beta)-F(\alpha_{j-1}-x_i^\top\beta),
$$
with $\alpha_0=-\infty$ and $\alpha_3=\infty$. The frequencies enter as weights.

```{r housing-ordinal, eval=has_mass}
housing <- MASS::housing
ord <- fastglm_ordinal(Sat ~ Infl + Type + Cont, data=housing, weights=Freq)
```

```{r housing-ordinal-tidy, eval=has_broom}
tidy(ord)
glance(ord)
```

The modes of *emmeans* for ordinal fits are those it provides for `MASS::polr()`. With `mode="prob"`, the grid gains the outcome category as a factor, and each estimate is a category probability averaged over the grid cells:

```{r housing-ordinal-prob, eval=has_emmeans}
emmeans(ord, ~ Sat | Infl, mode="prob")
```

With `mode="mean.class"`, the estimate is the mean category number $\sum_j j\,P(Y=j\mid x)$, averaged over the grid, which places the three influence levels on one scale:

```{r housing-ordinal-mean, eval=has_emmeans}
pairs(emmeans(ord, "Infl", mode="mean.class"))
```

The covariance of an ordinal fit is the inverse of the expected information, while `MASS::polr()` and `ordinal::clm()` use the observed information, so these standard errors can differ from theirs by a few percent.

`augment()` keeps the matrix column `.fitted` of category probabilities and adds one column `.prob_<level>` per category:

```{r housing-ordinal-augment, eval=has_broom}
head(augment(ord)[c("Sat","Infl","Type","Cont",".prob_Low",".prob_Medium",".prob_High",".class")], 3)
```

# Unordered satisfaction: multinomial probabilities

Treating `Sat` as unordered gives the baseline-category logit model, with low satisfaction as the reference category:
$$
P(Y_i=k\mid x_i)=\frac{\exp(x_i^\top\beta_k)}{\sum_{l=1}^{3}\exp(x_i^\top\beta_l)},\qquad \beta_1=0 .
$$
This model has a separate coefficient vector for each non-reference category, 14 coefficients in all against 8 parameters for the proportional odds model.

```{r housing-multinom, eval=has_mass}
housing_unordered <- transform(housing, Sat=factor(Sat, ordered=FALSE))
mn <- fastglm_multinom(Sat ~ Infl + Type + Cont, data=housing_unordered,
                       weights=Freq)
```

```{r housing-multinom-broom, eval=has_broom}
glance(mn)
head(augment(mn)[c("Sat","Infl",".prob_Low",".prob_Medium",".prob_High",".class")], 3)
```

The *emmeans* modes are those of `nnet::multinom()`: `"prob"` (the default) and `"latent"`.

```{r housing-multinom-prob, eval=has_emmeans}
sat_mn <- emmeans(mn, ~ Sat | Infl, mode="prob")
sat_mn
```

These probabilities are close to those of the proportional odds model (the largest difference is below), and the proportional odds model, with 6 fewer parameters, has the lower AIC:

```{r housing-compare, eval=has_emmeans}
sat_ord <- emmeans(ord, ~ Sat | Infl, mode="prob")
max(abs(summary(sat_mn)$prob - summary(sat_ord)$prob))
AIC(ord, mn)
```

A contrast within each category compares the influence levels on the probability scale; here, each level is compared with low influence:

```{r housing-multinom-contrast, eval=has_emmeans}
contrast(emmeans(mn, ~ Infl | Sat, mode="prob"), "trt.vs.ctrl")
```

The degrees of freedom of 14 follow the convention of `nnet::multinom()` in *emmeans* (the number of coefficients).

# Logistic regression in a tidymodels workflow

`birthwt` records whether each of 189 infants weighed less than 2.5 kg at birth (`low`), with the mother's age, weight (`lwt`), race, smoking status, number of previous premature labors (`ptl`), hypertension (`ht`), and uterine irritability (`ui`). The logistic model is
$$
\operatorname{logit} P(Y_i=\text{normal}\mid x_i)=x_i^\top\beta .
$$
As with the `"glm"` engine, the model is for the probability of the second level of the outcome factor. With the levels `low` and `normal`, *yardstick* treats the first level, `low`, as the event.

```{r birthwt-data, eval=has_tidymodels}
bw <- MASS::birthwt
bw <- data.frame(
    low=factor(bw$low, levels=c(1, 0), labels=c("low", "normal")),
    age=bw$age, lwt=bw$lwt, ptl=bw$ptl,
    race=factor(bw$race, labels=c("white", "black", "other")),
    smoke=factor(bw$smoke, labels=c("no", "yes")),
    ht=factor(bw$ht, labels=c("no", "yes")),
    ui=factor(bw$ui, labels=c("no", "yes")))
```

A recipe codes the factors as indicator columns, and `set_engine("fastglm")` selects fastglm for `logistic_reg()`:

```{r birthwt-workflow, eval=has_tidymodels, warning=FALSE}
library(parsnip)
library(recipes)
library(workflows)
rec <- recipe(low ~ ., data=bw) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
wf <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(rec) |>
    add_model(logistic_reg() |> set_engine("fastglm"))
wf_fit <- fit(wf, data=bw)
tidy(extract_fit_engine(wf_fit))
head(predict(wf_fit, bw, type="prob"), 3)
```

The coefficients are on the log odds of a normal birth weight, so a negative coefficient, as for smoking, lowers the probability of a normal weight. `extract_fit_engine()` returns the fastglm fit, with all of its methods. Engine arguments are given to `set_engine()`: `method` (the decomposition), `firth=TRUE` for mean bias reduction, `link`, and `threads`. An engine fit uses one thread unless `threads` is given, since resampling and tuning can run several fits at once in separate processes.

Five-fold cross-validation, stratified by the outcome, estimates out-of-sample accuracy, the Brier score, and the area under the ROC curve:

```{r birthwt-resamples, eval=has_tidymodels, warning=FALSE}
library(rsample)
library(tune)
set.seed(2)
folds <- vfold_cv(bw, v=5, strata=low)
res <- fit_resamples(wf, folds)
collect_metrics(res)
```

The same resamples with the `"glm"` engine give the same metrics, to rounding error:

```{r birthwt-glm, eval=has_tidymodels, warning=FALSE}
wf_glm <- update_model(wf, logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm"))
res_glm <- fit_resamples(wf_glm, folds)
max(abs(collect_metrics(res)$mean - collect_metrics(res_glm)$mean))
```

A bias-reduced fit changes only the engine argument:

```{r birthwt-firth, eval=has_tidymodels, warning=FALSE}
wf_firth <- update_model(wf, logistic_reg() |> set_engine("fastglm", firth=TRUE))
coef(extract_fit_engine(fit(wf_firth, data=bw)))
```

# Marginal effects with marginaleffects

Support for fastglm fits in *marginaleffects* is being contributed to that package. Until it is available there, `fastglm_marginal_effects()` and `fastglm_average()` compute average marginal effects and averaged predictions, with delta-method standard errors, for GLMs, count, two-part, ordinal, and multinomial fits, including streamed fits.
